prompt: Order the three tiers from where the machines plug in to the middle of the network.
hint: pc1 is at the bottom of the figure.
trap: Distribution sits between the two: it is the gateway of the access LANs and is cabled up to the core.

prompt: Which tier is the gateway of each access LAN and the place where rules about who may talk are applied?
hint: In the lab it is d1 and d2.

choices.text: Access
choices.why: Access switches connect machines and nothing else; a1 runs no routing.

choices.text: Distribution
choices.why: Right. d1 is pc1's gateway, 10.20.11.1, and the natural place for rules.

choices.text: Core
choices.why: The core carries everybody's traffic and is kept free of filtering for that reason.

choices.text: The hosts themselves
choices.why: Hosts can filter their own traffic, and they are not a tier of the network design.

prompt: How many OSPF neighbours did the core router c1 list?
hint: One line per neighbour.

prompt: pc1's traceroute to pc2 printed 10.20.11.1, 10.20.0.13, 10.20.0.18 and 10.20.12.22. Why does the access switch a1 not appear?
hint: What does traceroute count?

choices.text: a1 had been switched off
choices.why: Then pc1 would have reached nothing; its cable to d1 runs through a1.

choices.text: a1 has the address 10.20.11.1
choices.why: 10.20.11.1 is d1, pc1's gateway, in the first line.

choices.text: A switch is not a hop
choices.why: Right. traceroute counts routers, which decrement the TTL; a switch does neither.

choices.text: a1 filters the probes traceroute sends to it
choices.why: Nothing in the campus filters; a1 simply never decrements a TTL.

prompt: Somebody proposes letting the core routers also filter traffic between departments, to save a box. What does the hierarchy say about it?
hint: Whose traffic does the core carry?

choices.text: Keep it in distribution: whatever slows the core slows everyone
choices.why: Right. The core carries every block's traffic, so work that could slow or break it belongs a tier lower.

choices.text: Fine, since the core sees every packet and can judge it
choices.why: Seeing every packet is exactly why a mistake there reaches every department at once.

choices.text: Move it to the access switches, closer to people
choices.why: Access switches connect machines; rules about LANs talking belong where the LANs meet, in distribution.

choices.text: Fine, if a third core router is added for it
choices.why: A third core still carries everybody's traffic; the objection is about the tier, not the count.

prompt: d1's route to 10.20.12.0/24 lists `nexthop via 10.20.0.5 dev eth1 weight 1` and `nexthop via 10.20.0.13 dev eth2 weight 1`. What does that mean?
hint: Two lines, the same weight.

choices.text: Two paths of equal cost, through c1 and c2, both in use
choices.why: Right. OSPF installed both, and d1 spreads its traffic across the two cores.

choices.text: The second is a backup, used after the first fails
choices.why: Equal weights mean both are used now; a backup would not be installed beside the first.

choices.text: d1 sends every packet twice, once to each core
choices.why: Each packet takes one of the two; nothing is duplicated.

choices.text: OSPF has not finished choosing between them
choices.why: The lab had converged; two equal paths is the answer OSPF chose, not a pause.

prompt: pc1 sent 20 pings while d1's cable to c2 was cut. How many were lost?
hint: Read the summary line.

prompt: Lesson 3's ring lost 19 of 30 pings to a cut; d1 lost none of 20. Both labs use the same fast OSPF timers. What made the difference?
hint: Was the second path known before the cut?

choices.text: The campus cables carry data faster
choices.why: The lab's virtual cables carry no delay in either scenario.

choices.text: d1 already had the other path
choices.why: Right. Equal-cost multipath had both next hops installed, so d1 only dropped one; the ring had to compute a new path.

choices.text: Twenty pings are too few for any to be lost
choices.why: A loss would show in twenty as easily as in thirty; the ring lost most of its first twenty.

choices.text: The campus runs a different routing protocol
choices.why: Both run OSPF, with the same timers, as ring.sh and campus.sh say.

prompt: Which of these are redundant on paper and not in a failure? Choose all that apply.
hint: Shared fate, an unused path, capacity.

choices.text: Two uplinks laid in the same duct
choices.why: Right: one digger cuts both.

choices.text: Two equal-cost paths through separate cores, both carrying traffic
choices.why: That is the campus, and the cut showed it working.

choices.text: A backup link that has carried no traffic for a year
choices.why: Right: nothing says whether it still works until the day it has to.

choices.text: Two cores, each running at 70% of its capacity
choices.why: Right: when one fails, the other is asked for 140%.

choices.text: Two routers on separate power, tested each month
choices.why: Independent and exercised: that is redundancy in the failure as well.

prompt: When OSPF installs two paths of the same cost to one destination, the name in English is equal-cost ___.
hint: One word, several paths.

prompt: With d1 down, pc1 cannot reach even 10.20.11.1, while c1, c2 and d2 are healthy. Why does the doubled core not help?
hint: Walk up from pc1.

choices.text: The core takes a minute to notice d1 is gone
choices.why: Waiting would change nothing: pc1's packets never get past its dead gateway.

choices.text: pc2 went down with d1
choices.why: pc2 is under d2, which is healthy.

choices.text: OSPF on pc1 lost its neighbours
choices.why: pc1 runs no OSPF; it has a default route to its gateway.

choices.text: pc1's one way out is d1, below the core
choices.why: Right. The redundancy starts a tier too high for pc1: its gateway has no twin.

prompt: Match each part of the campus to what its failure takes down.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.right: Everyone on a1, and their way out

pairs.left: One of d1's two cables to the core
pairs.right: Nothing: the other cable carries it

prompt: The standard protocol that lets two routers share one gateway address, with one active and one on standby, is ___.
hint: Four letters; Cisco's equivalent is HSRP.

prompt: Which single point of failure do most networks accept rather than double?
hint: How many people notice, and how fast is the fix?

choices.text: The gateway of a floor's LAN
choices.why: Its failure reaches everyone on that LAN; it is what VRRP exists for.

choices.text: A desk PC's cable
choices.why: Right. It reaches one person, and a new patch cable fixes it in minutes.

choices.text: The pair of core routers
choices.why: The core reaches everyone; it is doubled in almost every network bigger than an office.

choices.text: The network connection of a shared server
choices.why: A server reaches everybody who uses it, so its connection is a candidate for two cards and LACP.

prompt: How did the lab show VRRP keeping pc1's gateway alive?
hint: Read the section's warning.

choices.text: It was not run in the lab
choices.why: Right. VRRP was described and drawn, not run; the scenario keeps one gateway so the failure could be shown.

choices.text: d2 took over 10.20.11.1 when d1 failed
choices.why: d2 has no cable to pc1's LAN, and pc1's pings to 10.20.11.1 were all lost.

choices.text: pc1 switched its gateway to 10.20.12.1
choices.why: That is pc2's gateway, on another LAN that pc1 cannot reach directly.

choices.text: c1 answered for 10.20.11.1 until d1 came back
choices.why: c1 is two tiers up and has no cable to pc1's LAN.

prompt: c1's `ip route` printed 11 lines. How many routes does the table hold?
hint: Lines starting with a tab continue the route above them.

prompt: How many /30 links fit in 10.20.0.0/24?
hint: 256 addresses, four per link.

prompt: Every LAN in the campus is a /24 inside 10.20.0.0/16. What does that buy?
hint: Think about the rest of the company's routers.

choices.text: Each PC gets more addresses of its own
choices.why: A PC has one address either way; the plan is about how routes add up.

choices.text: A /24 network forwards faster than other sizes
choices.why: The size of a prefix does not change how fast a router forwards.

choices.text: The whole campus is one route to the rest
choices.why: Right. Blocks that line up let 10.20.0.0/16 stand for every LAN in it.

choices.text: OSPF refuses networks of other sizes
choices.why: OSPF carries the campus's /30 links as well as its /24 LANs.

prompt: A new building joins the campus with its own distribution pair and access switches, cabled to the core. In a design that scales, what is reconfigured on d1 and d2?
hint: Growth by adding pieces, not by changing them.

choices.text: A cable from each to the new distribution pair
choices.why: Distribution routers connect up to the core, not sideways to each other's blocks.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The new block plugs into the core and OSPF tells everyone; the existing blocks are not touched.

choices.text: Their LANs are renumbered to make room
choices.why: A plan that summarises leaves room in advance; renumbering is what a poor plan forces.

choices.text: Their firewall rules are rewritten for each new floor
choices.why: That is the poor design the section describes, where every change touches everyone.

prompt: In c1's table, `proto ___` marks a route the router has because it holds an address on that cable.
hint: The other value in the table is ospf.

prompt: On d1, LLDP lists `Interface: eth2`, `SysName: c2`, `PortDescr: eth2`. What goes into the cable table?
hint: Interface is d1's side; the rest describes the far end.

choices.text: d1 eth2 to c1 eth2
choices.why: c1 is on d1's eth1, the block above.

choices.text: d1 eth2 to c2 eth2
choices.why: Right. The interface is d1's, and SysName and PortDescr name the device and port at the far end.

choices.text: c2 eth0 to a1 p24
choices.why: a1's p24 goes to d1's eth0, not to c2.

choices.text: d1 eth0 to c2 eth2
choices.why: d1's eth0 goes down to a1.

prompt: What does `TTL: 120` mean in an LLDP neighbour entry?
hint: A neighbour that goes quiet drops off the list.

choices.text: Hops the announcement may cross
choices.why: LLDP announcements stay on one cable; they are never forwarded.

choices.text: Days since the cable on that port was installed
choices.why: LLDP knows nothing about installation dates.

choices.text: How long d1 keeps the entry, in seconds
choices.why: Right. If d1 hears nothing for 120 seconds, the neighbour is dropped.

choices.text: The neighbour's OSPF cost
choices.why: LLDP and OSPF are separate; the cost is not in this output.

prompt: Match each question to the command in this lesson that answers it.
hint: Each section used one.

pairs.left: Who is at the other end of eth2?
Which routers does c1 exchange routes with?
How many lines does c1's routing table print?

prompt: The diagram on the wall shows d1's eth2 cabled to d2. LLDP on d1 says eth2 goes to c2, and `ip` says eth2 holds 10.20.0.14/30. What do you conclude?
hint: Two sources read from the network agree with each other.

choices.text: The diagram is right, since it was drawn with care
choices.why: Care on the day it was drawn says nothing about every change since.

choices.text: LLDP is confused by the lab's virtual cables
choices.why: LLDP and the address agree: 10.20.0.14 is d1's end of the d1–c2 link.

choices.text: The diagram is out of date
choices.why: Right. Two independent readings off the network agree, and the drawing does not.

choices.text: d1 has two cables on eth2
choices.why: An interface has one cable; LLDP would list a second neighbour if there were one.

prompt: Why do many networks switch LLDP off on ports that face users and visitors?
hint: What does it announce, and to whom?

choices.text: It tells anyone plugged in what the device is and what it is called
choices.why: Right. Between network devices that is documentation; towards a stranger's laptop it is a description of the network.

choices.text: It slows the port down
choices.why: An announcement every so often costs nothing a user would notice.

choices.text: It stops DHCP from working
choices.why: LLDP and DHCP do not interfere with each other.

choices.text: Users' PCs cannot read it
choices.why: Whether a PC reads it is not the concern; what the switch tells it is.

prompt: Walk up from pc1 and order what it depends on to reach pc2, nearest first.
hint: The traceroute, plus the switch it cannot see.
items: A core router, c1 or c2
trap: a1 comes before d1 even though traceroute never shows it: pc1's frames reach d1 through it.

prompt: One floor of a campus loses the network. On that floor's distribution router, LLDP no longer lists the floor's access switch, and the uplinks to the core are fine. Where is the fault?
hint: Which neighbour disappeared?

choices.text: In the core routers
choices.why: The uplinks are fine, and a core fault would reach every floor.

choices.text: Below the router, on the floor's uplink
choices.why: Right. The access switch went quiet on that cable: the switch, its power or the cable itself.

choices.text: In the cable from each PC on that floor to the switch
choices.why: A whole floor at once, and a neighbour missing upstream, point at what they share.

choices.text: In the address plan
choices.why: Addresses do not stop an LLDP announcement; a dead link does.

prompt: Which changes remove a single point of failure on pc1's way out? Choose all that apply.
hint: Below the core, where pc1's path is single.

choices.text: A second router sharing 10.20.11.1 with d1 through VRRP
choices.why: Right: the gateway gets a twin.

choices.text: A third core router
choices.why: The core is already doubled; pc1's single points are below it.

choices.text: A spare access switch on the shelf
choices.why: A spare shortens the outage; it does not stop a1's failure from cutting pc1 off.

choices.text: A second network card in pc1, cabled to a second access switch
choices.why: Right: pc1's cable and a1 stop being its only way to the gateway.

choices.text: A second cable between c1 and c2
choices.why: That doubles a link pc1 does not depend on.
